title: {{NAME}} and the League of Unlikely Heroes
moral: Every kind of strength matters when the right moment calls for it.

pages.content: The headquarters of the Patchwork League sat inside a hollowed-out thundercloud above the city, its floors made of polished obsidian and its walls forever flickering with maps of trouble in progress. {{NAME}} had been brought here by a mechanical pelican named GUST, whose wings were twin turbines that hummed like a satisfied engine. Stepping out of GUST's cargo hatch, {{NAME}} found himself standing in the enormous main hall, staring at a team that was, to put it kindly, unconventional. There was IRON-OWL, a robot built from salvaged circuit boards and fitted with enormous rotating eyes. There was Sergeant Bramble, a warthog in a starred captain's uniform, with a jaw like a cornerstone and a stare that could stop traffic. And there, grooming her whiskers with elaborate calm, was Flicker, a tiny red squirrel who was also, inexplicably, the strongest creature in twelve time zones. The trouble bell was already ringing.

pages.content: IRON-OWL rotated its enormous eyes to focus on {{NAME}}, and the lenses cycled through seven colours before settling on a warm amber. 'New recruit assessed,' it said. 'Courage rating: high. Shoelace: untied.' {{NAME}} looked down. The shoelace was indeed untied. He tied it quickly, which seemed to impress IRON-OWL greatly. Sergeant Bramble crossed his thick arms and looked {{NAME}} up and down with deep scepticism. 'You're smaller than the last recruit,' the warthog said. 'The last recruit got frightened of the cloud ceiling and wouldn't come out from under the desk for a week,' said Flicker without looking up from her whiskers. Bramble made a noise like a lorry engine clearing its throat. Then the trouble screens flared red. A runaway weather machine, built by someone careless and clever in equal measure, was rolling down Coppergate Valley below, pulling fences, trees, and a rather startled flock of geese along with it. 'All units,' said Bramble, his scepticism evaporating instantly. 'Move.'

pages.content: The weather machine was the size of a small house, all churning cogs and spitting sparks, dragging a screaming wake of wind and debris through the valley. IRON-OWL swooped in first, its rotating eyes scanning for a shutdown switch. 'Located,' it announced, 'but access requires a grip-strength rating of four hundred kilograms.' Flicker was already moving. She blurred across three rooftops, leaped from a chimney stack, landed on the machine's bucking roof, and wrenched the emergency brake lever out of its casing with one paw as casually as pulling a carrot from soft soil. The machine shuddered, groaned, and began to slow. But the flock of geese, twelve of them, still tumbled through the air in a confused, honking tornado directly above the valley. Bramble looked at {{NAME}}. 'The geese need to be herded to the field on the east bank before they scatter,' he said. 'IRON-OWL can't herd. Flicker is busy. I'm too slow on foot in an open field.' {{NAME}} looked at the geese. They were frantic, spiralling. He took a breath, stepped forward, and began to call to them in a voice steady and calm as still water.

pages.content: One by one, the geese tilted their heads toward that calm voice, the way a ship turns toward a lighthouse. The leader, a large grey gander with a suspicious eye, circled lower, then lower still. {{NAME}} kept talking, patient and sure, describing the green field on the east bank, the quiet water, the peace waiting there. The gander landed beside him, studied him for one long moment with that suspicious eye, and then waddled eastward. The others followed, as geese always follow their leader, and within minutes all twelve were settled in the riverside grass, preening with great self-importance as if they had intended this all along. Sergeant Bramble stood at {{NAME}}'s shoulder, and the warthog's face had done something entirely new. 'I have stopped three runaway trains,' said Bramble quietly. 'I have never once thought of using my voice.' Flicker appeared on Bramble's shoulder, still not even slightly out of breath. 'That,' she said, 'is because you're very loud and geese do not respond well to very loud.' Bramble made the lorry-engine noise again, but this time there was something warm underneath it.

pages.content: Back at headquarters, in the low amber glow of the evening maps, the Patchwork League ate together at a long table made from cloud-stuff that was surprisingly good at holding plates. IRON-OWL produced a flask of extremely precise hot chocolate, measured to exactly the right temperature and sweetness for each team member. Flicker ate twelve walnuts in the time it took everyone else to sit down. Sergeant Bramble straightened his starred uniform, looked at {{NAME}}, and gave one brief, decisive nod, the sort of nod that means more than most speeches. {{NAME}} sat between Flicker and IRON-OWL, warm and pleasantly tired, listening to the rain patter against the cloud-walls outside. He was almost certainly the only person in the world doing homework at a table made of cloud, between a squirrel and a robot owl. He closed his eyes and thought that was perfectly fine by him. Somewhere below the cloud, he was almost sure he could hear the geese still arguing about which one of them had been most brave today.
